Supervised filter that scores each feature against a target

Source: R/fs_supervised.R
fs_supervised.Rd

Scores every column of data except target against the target, one feature at a time, and keeps or drops each feature by comparing its score with threshold. A numeric target is scored by absolute Pearson correlation, a categorical target by the one-way ANOVA F statistic.

Usage

fs_supervised(
  data,
  target,
  method = c("auto", "correlation", "anova"),
  threshold = 0,
  direction = c("above", "below"),
  action = c("keep", "remove"),
  include_equal = FALSE,
  na_rm = TRUE,
  output = c("result", "matrix", "dt", "data.frame", "mask", "indices", "names", "list"),
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame, data.table, or matrix holding target and the candidate features. Every column other than target must be numeric. The input is copied, never modified in place.

target

Single string naming the target column of data. The target may be numeric, factor, character, or logical; any other type is an error. It is removed from the candidates and used only for scoring.

method

One of "auto" (default), "correlation", or "anova". See Details.

threshold

Non-negative, finite number compared with each feature's score. Default 0. The scale depends on the method: [0, 1] for "correlation", [0, Inf] for "anova". With the defaults (threshold = 0, direction = "above", action = "keep") nothing is filtered: any non-constant feature, pure noise included, has a sample \(|r| > 0\) or \(F > 0\), so every feature with a defined score is kept. Set a threshold to make a real selection.

direction

"above" (default) or "below": which side of threshold a score must fall on to meet the condition.

action

"keep" (default) retains the features that meet the condition; "remove" drops them.

include_equal

Logical. If TRUE, a score equal to threshold meets the condition. Default FALSE.

na_rm

Logical. If TRUE (the default), rows with NA in a feature or in the target are left out when that feature is scored. If FALSE, an NA anywhere in a feature or in the target makes that feature's score NA.

output

Shape of the return value. "Candidate features" means the columns of data other than target, in their original order.

  • "result" (default): an fs_result object (see Value).

  • "matrix", "dt", "data.frame": the selected features as a numeric matrix, a data.table, or a data.frame.

  • "mask": logical vector with one element per candidate feature, named after the candidates; TRUE marks a selected feature.

  • "indices": integer positions of the selected features among the candidates (that is, in data without target), named after the selected features.

  • "names": character vector of the selected feature names.

  • "list": a list with filtered (matrix), mask, indices, names, scores, and meta. meta records method_arg (the method as requested), method_used (after "auto" is resolved), threshold, direction, action, include_equal, na_rm, n_input_cols, and n_kept_cols.

verbose

Logical; print progress messages. Default FALSE.

Value

With output = "result" (the default), an fs_result object:

  • selected: character vector of selected feature names.

  • scores: named numeric vector with one score per candidate feature, in column order, NA where the score is undefined.

  • method: "supervised_" followed by the method actually used, for example "supervised_correlation".

  • task: "regression" for a numeric target, "classification" for a factor target, and NA for a character or logical target, whose intended task is ambiguous.

  • model: NULL.

  • details: a list holding, in this order, mask (the logical keep-mask over the candidates), indices (selected positions, named), filtered (the selected columns as a data.table), threshold, direction, action, and n_features (the number of candidates, ncol(data) - 1).

  • call: the matched call.

Any other output returns the shape described under output.

When no feature meets the criteria, a warning is issued and the tabular shapes come back empty. "matrix" and "data.frame" then have zero columns and keep the input row count. The "dt" shape and details$filtered have zero columns and also zero rows, because data.table represents a zero-column table that way.

Details

No model is fitted, so the cost grows linearly with the number of columns and the function copes with wide data. Each feature is scored on its own, which has two consequences: the filter cannot see interactions, and it keeps every member of a group of near-duplicate columns that all track the target. Prune that redundancy afterwards with fs_correlation(), or use a wrapper such as fs_recursivefeature() or fs_svm() when the joint contribution of features is what you care about.

The three values of method:

  • "correlation" requires a numeric target. The score is the absolute Pearson correlation, in [0, 1]. A constant feature or a constant target has no defined correlation and scores NA. The constancy check is relative to each column's magnitude, so a feature measured on a very small or very large scale is scored normally.

  • "anova" requires a factor, character, or logical target. The score is the one-way ANOVA F statistic, in [0, Inf]. A feature that separates the classes perfectly (no spread within any class) scores Inf, and a constant feature scores NA.

  • "auto" (the default) uses "correlation" for a numeric target and "anova" otherwise. The two scales differ, so a threshold that suits one is meaningless for the other; with verbose = TRUE a message reports which method was chosen.

A feature whose score is NA is never selected, whether action is "keep" or "remove", and a warning reports how many features were excluded this way.

Columns are subset by position, never by name, so duplicated feature names cannot pull in the wrong column. The target's name must be unique, and every column needs a non-empty, non-NA name. A matrix keeps its own column names; V1, V2, ... are used only when it has none.

See also

The Filter methods guide, which runs this function on a worked example.

Examples

df <- data.frame(
  strong = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  mirror = c(4, 3, 2, 1),
  weak   = c(1, 0, 1, 0),
  y      = c(1, 2, 3, 4)
)

# Default: an fs_result
res <- fs_supervised(df, target = "y", method = "correlation",
                     threshold = 0.5)
res$selected
#> [1] "strong" "mirror"
res$scores
#>    strong    mirror      weak 
#> 1.0000000 1.0000000 0.4472136 
res$details$filtered
#>    strong mirror
#>     <num>  <num>
#> 1:      1      4
#> 2:      2      3
#> 3:      3      2
#> 4:      4      1

# The classic shapes are still available
fs_supervised(df, target = "y", method = "correlation", threshold = 0.5,
              output = "names")
#> [1] "strong" "mirror"

# ANOVA against a factor target
df_fac <- data.frame(
  wide = c(1, 2, 10, 11),
  mild = c(1, 3, 2, 4),
  grp  = factor(c("a", "a", "b", "b"))
)
fs_supervised(df_fac, target = "grp", method = "anova", threshold = 1,
              output = "matrix")
#>      wide
#> [1,]    1
#> [2,]    2
#> [3,]   10
#> [4,]   11
